secs.t: The Solar System and the planets · Revision points (22)

x: Source:
General Geography – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #1 (pp 2-11)
Earth is the
third
planet from the Sun, after Mercury and Venus.
The Solar System now has eight planets, since the IAU reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet in 2006.
Neptune is the farthest planet from the Sun.
Three are terrestrial: Mercury, Venus and Mars.
Mercury and Venus have no natural satellites.
The Solar System has the Sun, eight planets, dwarf planets, moons and small bodies, and there were nine planets before Pluto's 2006 reclassification.
Gravity keeps bodies in orbit.
The outer planets in order are Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
Jupiter
, the most massive planet, has the highest surface gravity, about 24.8 m/s².
Mercury is 57.9 million km from the Sun.
Jupiter 778.5, Saturn 1,432, Uranus 2,867 and Neptune 4,515 million km from the Sun.
Jupiter has a diameter of 142,984 km.
Neptune has a diameter of 49,528 km.
Mercury is
across.
Mercury revolves around the Sun in 88 days.
Jupiter takes 11.86 years, Saturn 29.4, Uranus 84.07 and Neptune 164.9 years to orbit.
Neptune has the longest revolution period at 165 years.
Mercury
, closest to the Sun, has the fastest orbital speed, about 47.9 km/s.
Venus is known as the Earth-twin.
Mars
is the Red Planet because iron oxide colours its surface.
The shape of Earth is a geoid or oblate spheroid.
Mercury is smallest, Venus hottest because of its thick CO2 greenhouse, Jupiter largest and Earth densest at about 5.5 g/cm³.

x: Source:

Earth rotates from west to east.
The Sun is overhead at the equator on 21 March.
NIFE stands for nickel (Ni) and iron (Fe, ferrum), the main metals of Earth's core.
Perihelion is when Earth is closest to the Sun.
The centrifugal force is maximum at the equator.
Earth’s equatorial diameter is 12,756 km.
Earth’s revolution produces a year and seasons.
Earth’s mean distance from the Sun is 149.6 million km.
Earth’s habitable zone is called the Goldilocks Zone.
Earth is the only known life-supporting planet.
Earth’s revolution occurs around the Sun.
Spring begins in the Northern Hemisphere on 21 March.
Autumn begins in the Northern Hemisphere on 23 September.
On 21 June the Sun is over the Tropic of Cancer (northern summer, southern winter), and on 22 December over the Tropic of Capricorn.
Day and night are approximately equal during the equinoxes.
The Sun contains 99.8% of the Solar System’s mass.
Earth reaches perihelion in early January.
One AU is the mean Earth–Sun distance of 149.6 million km (149.6 × 10⁹ m), which light crosses in about 8 min 19 s.
The shape of Earth is a geoid or oblate spheroid.
The crust is about 46.6% oxygen, 27.72% silicon, 8.13% aluminium and 5% iron.
The mantle lies below the crust.
Aryabhata explained the Sun's daily motion by Earth's rotation, Thumba was chosen for India's rocket station because it lies near the magnetic equator, and Earth Day (22 April) began in 1970.

secs.t: The Sun · Revision points (5)

x: Source:
General Geography – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #1 (pp 2-11)
The Sun is a star at the centre of the Solar System.
The Sun's plasma core is about 15 million °C, where fusion turns hydrogen into helium and releases energy.
The corona is visible during a solar eclipse.
The Sun is the closest star to Earth.
Auroras form when charged solar particles strike gases in the upper atmosphere near the magnetic poles.

secs.t: The Moon and eclipses · Revision points (13)

x: Source:
General Geography – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #1 (pp 2-11)
A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth.
By the calendar definition, a Blue Moon is the second full moon in one month.
The Moon’s diameter is 3,475 km.
The Moon shows the same face toward Earth.
Perigee is the Moon’s closest position to Earth.
Apollo 11 landed in the
Sea of Tranquility
In a solar eclipse the Moon's shadow falls on Earth and is seen in a narrow region, and in a lunar eclipse Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
The Moon’s atmosphere is essentially absent.
A lunar eclipse is seen across the night side and turns the Moon reddish, while the corona shows during a total solar eclipse.
Full moon has Earth between Sun and Moon, new moon has the Moon between Sun and Earth, and half moon has a 90° angle.
At perigee, the Moon produces stronger gravity and higher tides.
The lunar (synodic) month is about
29.5 days
Sunlight takes 8 minutes 19 seconds to reach Earth.

Copernicus proposed the heliocentric model.
The main asteroid belt lies
between Mars and Jupiter
A meteoroid is a small rocky or metallic body in space.
Halley’s Comet is a short-period comet.
Apollo 11
made the first crewed Moon landing in 1969.
Asteroids are composed of rock and metal.
Comets come from the Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud and grow tails pointing away from the Sun when near it, while asteroids lack tails.
Near the Sun a comet develops a coma and a tail of dust and ionised gas.
Radiation pressure and solar wind direct a comet’s tail away from the Sun.
A meteor is the streak of light called a
shooting star
Galileo studied the Galilean moons.
Johann Galle first observed
Neptune
Halley’s Comet last appeared in 1986.

secs.t: Rotation — day, night and time · Revision points (20)

x: Source:

Earth turns once on its axis in about
24 hours
The Coriolis effect deflects moving objects
to the right
in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern.
Earth rotates west to east, counter-clockwise when seen from above the North Pole.
The Coriolis effect is zero or absent at the Equator.
The main result of Earth’s rotation is day and night.
Earth completes a full rotation of 360° in 24 hours.
Rotation produces time zones.
Earth's two motions are rotation, its spin on its axis, and revolution, its elliptical path around the Sun.
Earth’s axis is an imaginary line joining the North and South Poles.
Day is experienced by the part of Earth facing the Sun.
Earth rotates through 15° per hour.
The centrifugal effect is caused by Earth’s rotation.
Earth’s axis makes an angle of 66.5° with the orbital plane.
A is true: the Coriolis effect shapes cyclones.
The centrifugal effect causes equatorial bulging and polar flattening.
Weight is minimum at the Equator.
The length of day has changed by a very small measurable amount.
Ice-sheet melting redistributes mass and water toward lower latitudes.
Earth’s revolution produces seasons with axial tilt.
Heating is lower in winter.

secs.t: Revolution, orbit and the calendar · Revision points (20)

x: Source:
General Geography – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #2 (pp 11-19), #3 (pp 19-27)
One revolution around the Sun takes about
365.25 days
; 24 hours is one rotation.
Earth is at perihelion, nearest the Sun,
around 4 January
, and at aphelion around 4 July.
Earth’s revolution causes seasons along with axial tilt.
Earth’s axis remains approximately parallel during revolution.
Earth’s angular speed is 15° per hour.
A is true: Earth moves fastest at perihelion.
Earth moves on an elliptical orbit, takes about 365¼ days per revolution and so keeps changing its position around the Sun.
Earth is approximately 147 million km from the Sun at perihelion.
Earth’s orbital speed is greater at perihelion.
A normal calendar year has 365 days.
Rotation has an indirect seasonal role.
All three are needed: revolution, axial tilt and the axis staying parallel together produce the seasonal cycle.
Seasons occur because Earth revolves around the Sun and has an axial tilt of 23½°.
All four come from revolution with tilt: seasons, solstices and equinoxes, opposite seasons in the hemispheres and six-month polar day and night.
Earth’s axis is inclined 66½° to its orbital plane.
The hemispheres alternately tilt toward and away from the Sun.
Seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres, so summer in one means
winter
in the other.
Solstices and equinoxes each come twice a year, with the Sun over a tropic at a solstice and over the Equator at an equinox.
Perihelion occurs during the Northern Hemisphere’s winter period.
Distance from the Sun does not primarily cause seasons.

secs.t: Seasons — causes and solar angle · Revision points (14)

x: Source:
General Geography – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #3 (pp 19-27), #2 (pp 11-19)
Summer has direct rays and long days, and winter has slanting rays and short days.
Summer gets more solar energy and heating, and winter less.
On 21 June the Sun is overhead at the
Tropic of Cancer
The summer hemisphere receives more direct rays and longer days.
At an equinox, the Sun is overhead at the Equator.
The vertical Sun is at the Equator on 21 March.
The main consequence of Earth’s revolution and axial tilt is a changing angle of insolation during the year.
During summer, the hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun.
Day length, illumination and heating change through the year, and the changing heating gives seasons.
More oblique or slanting solar rays spread energy over a larger area and produce lower heating.
A higher Sun in the sky produces a smaller shadow.
At the equinoxes the Sun is
vertically overhead
at the Equator, so there is no noon shadow.
The Tropic of Cancer lies at 23½°N.
Direct rays concentrate energy on a small area, giving greater heating.

secs.t: Solstices and equinoxes · Revision points (15)

x: Source:
General Geography – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #2 (pp 11-19), #3 (pp 19-27)
The Northern Hemisphere has its longest day and shortest night on 21 June.
The order is March Equinox, June Solstice, September Equinox, December Solstice, that is D, B, A, C.
The Sun’s direct rays fall on the Tropic of Cancer at the June summer solstice.
Equinoxes come twice a year with equal day and night; in March spring starts in the north, and in September autumn.
The Sun is overhead at the Equator on 21 March.
The September equinox occurs approximately on 22 or 23 September.
Areas beyond the Arctic Circle experience continuous daylight during Northern Hemisphere summer.
The North Pole is tilted toward the Sun during the June solstice.
After 23 September, the Sun continues moving southward.
From September to December northern days shorten and southern days lengthen, and from December to March the reverse happens.
The Northern Hemisphere’s longest day usually occurs on 20 or 21 June.
With the Sun over Cancer the north has summer and its longest day while the south has winter, and with the Sun over Capricorn the south has summer.
Christmas is summer in Australia.
Seasonal contrast is maximum at a solstice.
Polar day lasts approximately six months.

secs.t: Latitudes, the Equator and the poles · Revision points (10)

x: Source:
General Geography – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #2 (pp 11-19), #3 (pp 19-27)
The Sun’s direct rays fall on the Tropic of Cancer at the June summer solstice.
The North Pole has six months of continuous daylight.
The Tropic of Cancer is at 23.5°N latitude.
At the Equator day and night are each about 12 hours all year.
Seasonal variation in day length is very small at the Equator.
The South Pole has continuous daylight around December.
Polar day lasts approximately six months.
The midnight sun occurs beyond the polar circles, peaks near each summer solstice, can give 24-hour daylight and is seen in Norway and other polar lands.
Polar day occurs because the 23½° axial tilt and revolution tilt a pole toward the Sun.
The angular distance from the Tropic of Cancer to the Tropic of Capricorn is 47°.

season

Rabi crops are sown in October or November.
Monsoonal winds reverse direction according to the season.
A
monsoon
is a seasonal reversal of winds.
The Indian southwest monsoon occurs from June to September.
The Indian traditional summer season lasts from May to June.
Kharif crops are harvested in October or November.
Mountain and valley breezes are periodic winds, summer heating makes low pressure and winter cooling makes high pressure.
Monsoonal climate has wet and dry seasons.
Seasonal crop cycles include Rabi, Kharif and Zaid crops.

mantle

Movement and convection of conducting material in the liquid outer core produce the geodynamo.
The core begins at about
depth, at the Gutenberg discontinuity.

Mantle heat causes convection or thermal movement.
A volcano releases lava, ash, and gases.
The mantle is composed mainly of magnesium–iron silicates.
The asthenosphere is mechanically weak and ductile, which is why plates can slide over it.

V-shaped valleys are formed by river erosion.

Barchans are crescent-shaped dunes.
A
stalagmite

Caves or caverns are underground dissolution features.
Mountains form by folding, faulting, volcanism and erosion.

Valleys are carved by rivers, glaciers, tectonic faulting and karst solution.

Yardangs are desert landforms.
Loess

Coastal landforms are formed by waves, currents, and tides.
Tectonic landforms such as rift valleys, horsts, grabens and fold mountains come from faulting, folding and crustal movement.
The Salt Range is a block mountain range.
The world’s highest peaks mostly occur in young fold mountains.
Gorges are deep, narrow, steep-sided river valleys.

An estuary

funnel-shaped tidal mouth

Andes

Volcanic mountains are formed by the accumulation of lava and volcanic material.

cones
